title: A Fleck of Paint at 17,500 mph Cracked a Space Station Window

scenes.text: A paint fleck at 17,500 miles an hour cracked this window.
In 2016, astronaut Tim Peake photographed a 7 millimetre chip in the glass.
scenes.keywords: International Space Station cupola window Earth

scenes.text: The culprit was a few thousandths of a millimetre across. Smaller than a speck of dust.
At orbital speed, speed is everything. A one centimetre bolt would punch through the station's shields.
Anything over 10 centimetres could shatter a satellite into pieces.
The window is quadruple glazed. The fleck only scratched the outer pane. This time.

description:
In 2016, astronaut Tim Peake photographed a 7-millimetre chip in a window of the International Space Station's Cupola, gouged out by a speck of debris, probably a paint flake, only a few thousandths of a millimetre across.
Orbital debris travels at roughly 17,500 miles an hour, so even a tiny speck hits hard. The European Space Agency says an object around one centimetre could penetrate the station's shields, and anything over 10 centimetres could shatter a satellite. The Cupola's windows have four layers; only the outer pane was damaged.
Would you still look out that window? Comment below.
first_comment: The station regularly fires its thrusters to dodge larger pieces of junk that radar can track. The small stuff, like this fleck, can't be tracked at all. Would you sign up for six months up there?
